html:
The Buddhas of Bamiyan were two giant standing Buddhas carved into a cliff in the Bamiyan valley of the Hindu Kush, in what is now Afghanistan, in the 6th and early 7th centuries. Carbon dating puts the smaller, 38 metres tall, at about 570 and the larger, 55 metres tall, at about 618.

Bamiyan lay on a route between Bactria and the plains of India, and the valley held many monasteries cut into the rock. The statues were made in the years when the Hephthalites and their successors ruled the area. Their style was a late form of the Buddhist art of Gandhara, which grew under the Kushans and blended Greek and Indian forms. The bodies were shaped in stone, then covered with clay and painted. Caves around them were painted too.

The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang passed through around 630 on his way to India and described the statues and a busy Buddhist community.

Islam spread through the region from the 9th century onward, and the monks left, but the statues stood for well over a thousand years more.

In March 2001 the Taliban government blew them up as idols, despite appeals from around the world. In the same years the Taliban killed many of the local Hazara people. The empty niches are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2003, and a reminder of how long Buddhism lasted along the Silk Road.
